title: Mortgage Payments Nearly Doubled Since 2021, Mostly Not From Prices
description:
US mortgage rates just hit their highest level in three years. We show why the monthly payment on a typical home nearly doubled since 2021, and how much of that came from prices versus rates.

Built on Census, Freddie Mac and Labor Department data with the standard loan formula, plus our honest take for buyers.
comment: If you have a mortgage, what rate did you lock in, and would you move house at today's rates?

scenes.narration: At the start of October, the average rate on a thirty-year mortgage in the United States climbed to {{ latest(rate_news) | pct1 }}. That is the highest since late 2023.

headlines.text: US Mortgage Rates Climb Further in October

scenes.narration: For anyone trying to buy a home, that number matters more than almost anything else, more even than the price on the listing. Here is why.

chart.title: Mortgage rates hit a three-year high
chart.label: WHAT JUST HAPPENED

scenes.narration: If you have looked at buying a home recently, you have probably noticed something strange. House prices went up, yes. But the monthly payment went up much, much more. In early 2021, the payment on a typical new home was about {{ payment(0.8 * value(price, "2021-01"), value(rate, "2021-01"), 30) | usd }} a month. In the latest data, it is about {{ payment(0.8 * latest(price), latest(rate), 30) | usd }}. Today we will find out exactly where that difference came from, using the official data and the same formula the banks use.

chart.title: Why did mortgage payments nearly double?
chart.label: HOUSING, IN NUMBERS

scenes.narration: Every monthly payment comes from just two ingredients: the price of the house and the interest rate on the loan.

chart.query: for sale sign house United States
chart.caption: Two ingredients: price and rate

scenes.narration: Start with the price. This is the median sales price of a new home in the United States, which means half of new homes sell for more and half for less. In early 2021 it was {{ value(price, "2021-01") | usd }}. In the latest data it is {{ latest(price) | usd }}. That is a rise of {{ pct_change(price, "2021-01", "latest") | pct }}. A big increase, but nowhere near double.

Now the second ingredient, the interest rate. This is the average rate on a thirty-year fixed mortgage, going back to 1971. It peaked at {{ highest(rate, "1971", "latest") | num }} percent in {{ year_of_highest(rate, "1971", "latest") | year }}, and then fell for four decades. In early 2021 it was only {{ value(rate, "2021-01") | num }} percent, close to the lowest ever recorded. Then, as the Federal Reserve fought inflation, it shot up. The latest reading is {{ latest(rate) | num }} percent.

Let's zoom in on the last few years, because that is where the whole story happens. Before the pandemic, rates were already low by historical standards. In December 2019, the average was {{ value(rate, "2019-12") | num }} percent. During the pandemic the Federal Reserve cut its own rate to almost zero and bought large amounts of mortgage bonds, which pushed mortgage rates to record lows. When inflation took off in 2021 and 2022, the Fed reversed course and raised its rate quickly. Mortgage rates followed, climbing as high as {{ highest(rate, "2021", "latest") | num }} percent. For anyone buying a home, that was one of the fastest rises in borrowing costs in decades.

chart.title: From record lows to a sharp climb
chart.subtitle: Thirty-year fixed mortgage rate, percent per year

scenes.narration: Let's turn those two numbers into a monthly payment. We assume a buyer puts twenty percent down and borrows the rest over thirty years, the most common setup. The standard loan formula then gives the monthly payment for interest and repayment. In early 2021, that was about {{ payment(0.8 * value(price, "2021-01"), value(rate, "2021-01"), 30) | usd }}. Today it is about {{ payment(0.8 * latest(price), latest(rate), 30) | usd }}. That is {{ payment(0.8 * latest(price), latest(rate), 30) / payment(0.8 * value(price, "2021-01"), value(rate, "2021-01"), 30) | times }} as much, for a house that costs only {{ pct_change(price, "2021-01", "latest") | pct }} more.

chart.title: Monthly payment on the median new home
chart.subtitle: Twenty percent down, thirty-year fixed loan, interest and repayment only

scenes.narration: Now the interesting part. We can split the increase in two with a simple model. First, keep the 2021 interest rate, but use today's price. That raises the payment by about {{ payment(0.8 * latest(price), value(rate, "2021-01"), 30) - payment(0.8 * value(price, "2021-01"), value(rate, "2021-01"), 30) | usd }} a month. That is the price effect. Then switch to today's interest rate. That adds another {{ payment(0.8 * latest(price), latest(rate), 30) - payment(0.8 * latest(price), value(rate, "2021-01"), 30) | usd }} a month. That is the rate effect. The rate effect is more than three times bigger. Your mortgage payment did not double because of house prices. It doubled mostly because of interest rates.

chart.title: Where the increase came from
chart.subtitle: Monthly payment, split into a price effect and a rate effect

scenes.narration: So when you sign for a loan, the rate you lock in can matter more than the price you negotiate.

Why do rates matter so much? Because on a thirty-year loan, most of your early payments are interest. Here is the payment on today's median home at different rates. At three percent, it would be about {{ payment(0.8 * latest(price), 3, 30) | usd }}. At five percent, about {{ payment(0.8 * latest(price), 5, 30) | usd }}. At seven percent, about {{ payment(0.8 * latest(price), 7, 30) | usd }}. Every extra point on the rate costs hundreds of dollars a month, for decades.

chart.title: Same house, different rates
chart.subtitle: Monthly payment on today's median new home

scenes.narration: Finally, let's measure it in time instead of dollars. In early 2021, the monthly payment took about {{ payment(0.8 * value(price, "2021-01"), value(rate, "2021-01"), 30) / value(wages, "2021-01") | num }} hours of work at the average hourly wage. Today it takes about {{ payment(0.8 * latest(price), latest(rate), 30) / latest(wages) | num }} hours. Pay went up too, but not nearly enough to keep up with the payment.

chart.title: Hours of work to pay one month's mortgage
chart.subtitle: Monthly payment divided by average hourly pay

scenes.narration: So, why did your mortgage payment nearly double? House prices did their part, but the main reason was the jump in interest rates, which more than doubled from close to the lowest ever recorded. Of the extra {{ payment(0.8 * latest(price), latest(rate), 30) - payment(0.8 * value(price, "2021-01"), value(rate, "2021-01"), 30) | usd }} a month, about {{ (payment(0.8 * latest(price), latest(rate), 30) - payment(0.8 * latest(price), value(rate, "2021-01"), 30)) / (payment(0.8 * latest(price), latest(rate), 30) - payment(0.8 * value(price, "2021-01"), value(rate, "2021-01"), 30)) | pct }} came from the higher rate. It also explains a puzzle. When rates rise, many current owners do not want to sell and give up their old, cheap mortgage. Fewer homes come up for sale, and that helps keep prices high too. For buyers, the practical lesson is simple. When you compare homes, compare monthly payments at today's rate, not just prices, because the rate can matter more than the sticker.

Here is my take. Waiting for prices to fall is the wrong focus for most buyers, because the rate does more of the damage. Prices rarely fall far, but rates can move a lot in a couple of years, and a loan can often be refinanced later if rates come down. That cuts both ways, though. Nobody knows where rates are going, so a payment only makes sense if you can afford it at today's rate. A few honest caveats. Real payments also include property tax and insurance, which we left out, and your own price, down payment and rate will be different.

chart.title: Watch the rate, not just the price
chart.label: MY TAKE

method: Monthly payments use the standard fixed-rate loan formula with twenty percent down over thirty years, on the median new-home price and the average thirty-year rate. To split the rise, we change the price first at the old rate, then the rate.
